questions.question: What does an audio sample rate of 16 kHz mean?
options: The file stores 16,000 bits per sample
The signal was measured 16,000 times per second
questions.explanation: Sample rate is the number of samples captured each second. The lesson uses this to connect sample index to time with t = n / sr and to explain why a 10-second clip at 16 kHz has 160,000 samples.

questions.question: What usually happens when a signal contains frequencies above the Nyquist limit for a given sample rate?
options: They fold into lower frequencies as aliasing
They become louder but stay at the same frequency
They are automatically converted into silence
They only change the phase, not the spectrum
questions.explanation: The lesson emphasizes that Nyquist is sr/2, the highest frequency that can be represented unambiguously. Energy above that limit aliases, meaning it appears as false lower-frequency content in the sampled signal.

questions.question: According to the lesson, how many samples are in a 10-second mono clip recorded at 16 kHz?
questions.explanation: A 16 kHz signal has 16,000 samples per second. Over 10 seconds, that becomes 160,000 samples, which the lesson uses as the canonical example for waveform length.

questions.question: For an N-point DFT, which formula maps frequency bin k to its frequency in Hz?
questions.explanation: The lesson states that DFT bin k corresponds to k · sr / N Hz. This mapping is what lets you convert the index of the dominant FFT peak back into a real-world frequency.

questions.question: Why do we apply a window such as Hann or Hamming before taking the FFT of short audio frames?
options: To remove edge discontinuities and reduce spectral leakage
To make the sample rate higher
questions.explanation: The lesson explains that we do not FFT the whole clip at once; we frame it and taper each frame with a window. That window suppresses discontinuities at the frame boundaries, which reduces leakage into neighboring frequency bins.
